figs.title: Eigenvectors as contour axes
figs.caption: The contours of a quadratic are ellipses centred on x* with principal axes along the eigenvectors of H. On the contour f = ½ the semi-axis along vᵢ has length 1/√λᵢ, so the smaller eigenvalue gives the longer axis.

figs.title: Saddle and the negative curvature direction
figs.caption: Mixed sign eigenvalues give hyperbolic contours around a saddle. Along the eigenvector with λ < 0 the function curves downward, so f decreases in both directions from x* along that line.

figs.title: Newton versus modified Newton on an indefinite model
figs.caption: With an indefinite B the Newton step goes to the stationary point of the model, which is a saddle and here points uphill. Modified Newton adds E so B + E is positive definite, which yields a descent direction.

figs.title: BFGS secant condition
figs.caption: BFGS picks B_{k+1} so that B_{k+1} s = y, matching the gradient change along the last step. In one dimension this makes B_{k+1} the secant slope of f′, and the curvature condition yᵀs > 0 keeps B positive definite.

figs.title: SQP linearizes the constraint at each iterate
figs.caption: SQP replaces the constraint by its tangent h_{k} + ∇h_{k}ᵀp = 0 and minimizes a quadratic model of the Lagrangian on that plane. The step lands on the linearization, and the curvature of h leaves a small residual for the next iteration to correct.

figs.title: Augmented Lagrangian conditioning
figs.caption: The quadratic penalty needs a large μ to approach x*, which stretches the contours and drives up the Hessian condition number. The augmented Lagrangian with λ at λ* reaches x* exactly at a moderate μ, so the subproblem stays well conditioned.

figs.title: Finite difference step size V curve
figs.caption: Forward difference truncation error grows like h and round off error grows like ε/h, so the total error on log axes forms a V. The best step sits near √ε, about 10⁻⁸ in double precision.

figs.title: Adjoint versus direct sensitivity cost
figs.caption: The direct method needs one linear solve per design variable and the adjoint method needs one per output. With many design variables and few outputs, as in aerodynamic shape design, the adjoint is far cheaper.

figs.title: Utopia and nadir points
figs.caption: The utopia point takes each objective at its individual minimum, and the nadir point takes the worst value of each objective over the Pareto front. Together they bound the front and give the scale for normalizing objectives.

figs.caption: Each generation evaluates fitness, selects parents, recombines them by crossover and mutates a few bits to form the next population. Selection exploits good designs while mutation keeps exploring.

figs.title: Exact versus inexact line search
figs.caption: An exact line search solves φ′(α) = 0 for the minimizing step, which costs many evaluations. An inexact search accepts any step in the strong Wolfe set, and the trial α = 1 of a Newton type method usually qualifies.

figs.title: Exact trust region step as the radius grows
figs.caption: The trust region solution follows p(λ) = −(B + λI)⁻¹g. For a small radius the step leaves along −g, and as Δ grows it bends toward the full Newton step, which the dogleg approximates with two straight legs.

figs.title: Multiplier as a shadow price
figs.caption: Shifting the constraint bound b moves the optimum, and the optimal objective changes at the rate df*/db = μ*. A large multiplier marks a constraint that is expensive to hold.

figs.title: Interpolation versus regression surrogates
figs.caption: An interpolating surrogate such as an RBF uses one weight per sample and passes through every point, which suits deterministic simulations. A regression surrogate with fewer basis functions minimizes the sum of squared residuals and smooths noisy data.
